taxonomy.note: Accepted in the current Kew/POWO Tradescantia backbone; learner retained at species rank.

evidence: Travis — UT Plant Resources Center Travis County Commelinaceae index includes Tradescantia occidentalis.
Williamson — UT Plant Resources Center provides a detailed local treatment of Tradescantia occidentalis.
Bexar — a research-grade iNaturalist record from Mud Creek Park in San Antonio supplies a supporting exact-county occurrence; the species is also documented in a Bexar County flora context.
target_zone_range.guardrail: PASS uses explicit county-level flora/herbarium or supporting occurrence evidence; no broad ecoregion statement is converted into an unnamed county.

morphology.look_here_first: Start with the narrow leaves and the stem hairs. Prairie spiderwort has narrow linear to strap-shaped leaves and conspicuous long-stalked glandular hairs on the internodes and peduncles. In the Williamson treatment the blades are only about 6–17 mm wide, which gives the plant a noticeably grassier look than giant spiderwort.
diagnostic_traits: ascending to suberect, about 15–65 cm in the Williamson treatment
internodes and peduncles conspicuously long-stalked glandular-hairy
narrow strap-shaped to linear leaves, about 6–17 mm wide locally
two conspicuous unequal leaflike bracts subtend the terminal paired cymes
sepals conspicuously glandular-hairy; flowers violet, blue, rose-violet or magenta

confusers.separator: T. gigantea is more robust and broader-leaved with lower stems essentially glabrous; T. occidentalis has obvious glandular stem hairs and narrower foliage.
T. humilis is much lower and bushier, with hairy leaf blades and dense basal branching; T. occidentalis is taller, grassier and strongly glandular on the stem/peduncle.

installation_guardrail: Strict PASS complete; install under standing blanket approval.
